run.question: We're running low on disk space. Can you check our application indexes (app-187-*) and identify which one is consuming the most storage? Please tell me the index name and approximately how much space it's using.

report.summary: Listing every index in the registered Elasticsearch/OpenSearch target for the pattern app-187-* returned 21 indices, and the same 21 were the only indices matching * in the target, so the set is complete for the name pattern. The largest by store size is app-187-metrics-analytics at 506.2kb (primary store size also 506.2kb) holding 5000 documents; the remaining 20 indices are app-187-logs-01 through app-187-logs-20, each holding 10 documents and about 9kb (app-187-logs-19 reports 9.1kb). Adding the returned values gives roughly 0.7 MB of index storage in total, so no index in app-187-* is consuming significant storage. Counter to the premise that disk space is being consumed here, the single node opspilot-m1-control-plane reported DiskPressure=False ('kubelet has no disk pressure') at query time. I could not check node filesystem free/used metrics because the Prometheus source returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so the actual disk consumption on the host is unknown and this answer cannot confirm or deny host-level disk pressure.

claims.text: The index app-187-metrics-analytics is the largest storage consumer among the app-187-* indices: store.size 506.2kb, pri.store.size 506.2kb, docs.count 5000, health green, status open.
The other 20 indices are app-187-logs-01 through app-187-logs-20, each with docs.count 10 and store.size 9kb, except app-187-logs-19 at 9.1kb; all 20 report health yellow and status open.

The target contains exactly 21 indices in total (indices_shown 21, indices_omitted 0), all named app-187-*; a wildcard * listing returned the same 21 indices, so no larger index exists under a different name in this target.
Summing the returned store.size values gives approximately 686 KB of total index storage (506.2kb for app-187-metrics-analytics plus ~180kb across the 20 app-187-logs-* indices).

The only node in the cluster, opspilot-m1-control-plane, reported condition DiskPressure=False with message 'kubelet has no disk pressure' (and MemoryPressure=False) at the time of the query, which does not corroborate a host disk-pressure condition on this cluster.

These app-187-* indices are small in absolute terms (hundreds of kilobytes, 5000 documents maximum in one index), so the index store itself is not supported as the source of low disk space by this evidence.

If disk space really is low, the consumer is more likely outside these Elasticsearch indices (for example container images, node container/runtime storage or Volume-level files), but this is unverified; I did not obtain node filesystem usage.

Before any remediation, obtain node-level filesystem free/used bytes (node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes equivalents) and container image and volume usage from the host, since the index sizes are far too small to explain a full disk.
If index cleanup is still desired, app-187-metrics-analytics (506.2kb, 5000 docs) is the only meaningful candidate among app-187-*, but deleting it would free well under 1 MB.

gaps: Node filesystem free/used space is unknown: the Prometheus metric discovery query for {__name__=~"node_filesystem.*|kubelet_volume.*"} returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no disk-capacity metric was read and host disk pressure cannot be quantified.
Storage reporting excludes any non-index disk consumers (container images, container writable layers, logs on the node) because no tool in this Run exposes them.

The index listing tool has no time range and reflects the state at query time (observed_at 2026-11-21T05:04:03Z and 2026-11-21T05:04:06Z); earlier index sizes or index deletions before those instants are unknown.
The persistentvolumeclaims query returned no rows (status no_data), so I cannot say whether any volume-backed storage exists or how large it is; absence in that single query is not a proven absence.
The store.size sort returned by the tool is lexicographic on the string values (9.1kb listed before 9kb), so I compared the returned values directly rather than relying on the tool's ordering.
next_steps: Collect node-level filesystem metrics (avail/size per device and mountpoint) from the host or from a working Prometheus/agent endpoint to identify the real disk consumer.
Check container image layer and container runtime storage on opspilot-m1-control-plane (e.g. kubelet/CRI image filesystem stats) and any emptyDir/volume usage in namespace otel-demo.
If index space policy is the concern, review retention and replicas for app-187-logs-* (20 yellow indices, each ~9kb) rather than expecting large savings from them.

view.cannot_prove: Objects are the cluster's state when the query ran, not during the incident window: they cannot prove what was true earlier, and an object missing now may have existed then. Events cover only their own timestamps inside the window; an event that is not returned is unknown, not proof nothing happened (events expire and timestamps are often null). A jq result is what the expression selected, not a full picture of the kind.

notes: This tool has no time range: it shows the cluster's indices and mappings at the moment of the query, which can be after the authorized window.
